 Spain Plans 5.3% Minimum Wage Rise for 2027 
 Milena Thomas Published Nov 5, 2026 
 Share: 
 Summary: 
 Spain's labor ministry proposes a 5.3% minimum wage increase for 2027 to €18,004 a year, equal to €1,286 per month when paid in 14 installments, affecting 2.5 million workers.
 The plan still needs the green light from Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's cabinet; the government had said it would set out the 2027 move before the Nov. 29 election.
 Unions pushed for 7%, employers did not sign on, and the figure is 0.4 percentage point above the level suggested by government-appointed experts.
 What is changing
 The labor ministry's proposal would lift Spain's minimum wage in 2027 to €18,004 per year, which is €1,286 a month on a 14-payment schedule. The ministry estimates about 2.5 million people would be covered. It is a 5.3% step up, and it will only take effect if Sánchez's cabinet signs off.
 This fits a broader arc: Sánchez has prioritized minimum wage hikes since taking office in 2018, when he first came in with the benchmark set at €10,302 annually, which works out to €735 each month. Spain heads into a Nov. 29 general election, and officials had said they would lay out the 2027 increase before voters go to the polls.

 Save my seat Politics and players
 The labor ministry is run by Sumar, the far-left coalition partner whose support has slumped ahead of the vote amid infighting over strategy. Built from several parties, Sumar has shifted into a new banner called Frente Amplio.
 Labor minister Yolanda Díaz leads Sumar and serves as one of Sánchez's deputy prime ministers. She is focusing on a bid to lead the International Labour Organization and will not be on the ballot in Spain.
 Smart investors treat new developments as prompts to refine their strategies and tools. We're hosting our first ever investor livestream on 11/17 to show you how to use ChatGPT and Claude to invest like a pro, hosted by Briefs Finance CEO Jaspreet Singh. Save your seat .
 Economy and negotiations
 Talks with unions and employers did not deliver a consensus on the 2027 figure. Unions sought a 7% climb, and the final number sits 0.4 percentage point above the recommendation from a panel of experts consulted by the government.
 Macro data gives Sánchez some cover. The Bank of Spain projects 2.6% growth this year, powered by domestic demand, a labor market buoyed by migration, and strong tourism. Its inflation outlook is 3.9% for this year and 3.7% for the following year.
 The broader backdrop for investors
 Political risk remains high. No poll shows Sánchez on course for another term after a series of crises, the latest being a rail crash last week that left 69 dead. It was the second such tragedy this year, and the transport minister resigned on Tuesday.
